author: Emma Honeybun
title: Feds declare Roberts Bank 2 expansion ‘project of national interest’
content:
A large-scale port expansion to be located off the coast of Delta, B.C., has been labelled as a ‘project of national interest,’ a designation which, according to environmental advocates, could result in the extinction of the Southern Resident Killer Whales.

In an email sent to APTN News on the heels of the announcement, Julia Levin, the associate director of national climate at Environmental Defence, wrote that not only is this “bad news for orcas,” but that it may be “a run-around on the Species at Risk Act, given that was the only approval that the project didn’t have.”

Robert Banks Terminal 2 is an expansion of the Port of Vancouver, operated by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority (VFPA) and located on 130 hectares (about 200 soccer pitches) of marine land off the B.C. coast.

According to a release from Ottawa, the project would add 2.4 million containers of annual capacity, increasing it by “approximately 50 per cent.”

It would also support “up to $100 billion in annual trade,” therefore “helping Canada achieve its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2035.”

It meets the criteria of what can be considered a project in the national interest, according to Bill C-5, the Building Canada Act, which are that it must “strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security”; “provide economic or other benefits”; “advance the interests of Indigenous Peoples”; and “contribute to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s climate change objectives.”

Once this criteria is met, major projects may be exempt from certain laws, such as the Species at Risk Act.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that, “By listing Roberts Bank Terminal 2 as a project of national interest, we are better connecting our economy with the world and diversifying our trade. As the world competes for capital, Canada will not wait. We are building a stronger, more independent, and more competitive Canadian economy.”

However, the project is also slated to be built in the Fraser River Estuary, which has already lost more than 85 per cent of floodplain habitat and supports 102 species at risk, according to Levin.

“The estuary is critical habitat for salmon and SRKW, southern resident killer whales, as confirmed by DFO and the environmental assessment of the project – which assessed that the new terminal would result in destruction of the legally protected Southern Resident Killer Whale’s critical habitat,” she wrote.

A 2020 environmental assessment for the project determined that it would cause “significant adverse environmental effects” on Chinook salmon, wetlands, and the resident whales, which have been listed as critically endangered since 2003.

An application for a Species at Risk permit, which would allow the building of the Roberts Bank 2 port in the habitat, was filed on Oct. 28, 2024, with a deadline of Oct. 28, 2026 — two days ago, as of publishing.

‘An incredible animal’: B.C. port expansion could drive southern resident killer whales to extinction, advocates warn

As of Friday morning, the tool used to track the permit’s progress on Canada’s website indicated it was overdue, but by the afternoon, the page had been wiped.

Canada held a consultation period while it considered the national interest designation, which began

In a letter sent to the Major Projects Office by Raincoast Conservation Foundation, the advocacy and research organization wrote that “Designation as a PONI is not an appropriate use of the Building Canada Act.

“Raincoast is concerned that the national interest cannot be reduced to container capacity, trade volume and construction speed when the proposal is in the Fraser River Estuary. Promises and investments announced by the federal government … to ensure prosperity by combining regulatory certainty with environmental protection are an insufficient guarantee given the level of harm identified from this project.”

Levin stated that, “by declaring this mega-port as a ‘project of national interest,’ Prime Minister Carney has dealt a devastating blow to the last remaining Southern Resident Killer Whales.

“This political moment will pass, but extinction is forever.”

She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Family of Miranda Mamakwa seeking criminal investigation into ‘negligent’ death of mother
content:
The family of a woman who died after a federal program did not arrange transportation to medical appointments is asking for a criminal investigation.

“The criminal justice system should only be invoked where grounds exist to believe a crime has been committed,” read the statement from the family. “Public officials are as accountable as anyone else in this country for reckless acts that endanger those in their charge.”

According to her family, Miranda Mamakwa died on Sept. 8 after she didn’t receive transportation to multiple important appointments following an open-heart surgery.

She was 31 and the mother of three kids.

“Literally, the blood of Indigenous people is required for any kind of meaningful change,” said Julian Falconer, legal counsel for the family. “We have created a pattern of behavior where we only get their attention once they [Canada] have killed somebody.”

Mamakwa was a member of Fort Severn First Nation, the northernmost community in Ontario, and was relying on transportation from the Non-Insured Health Benefits Program (NIHB) to get to follow-up appointments in Thunder Bay after her surgery in April 2026.

NIHB is a federal program provided by Indigenous Services Canada (ISC), and is mandated to provide medical transportation services, alongside other supports such as medication and vision care, to First Nations and Inuit people.

Her first appointment following her return home was scheduled for May 28, and the local nursing station had sent a request by fax (the only method of communication with NIHB offices available to them, Falconer confirmed) for NIHB to provide transportation.

However, the nearest office, located in Sioux Lookout, never got back to them.

Despite multiple requests and letters from her doctor, she missed four appointments, including “an appointment with a vascular surgeon about blood clots,” according to the backgrounder provided to the media.

The backgrounder also stated that, following the surgery, Mamakwa had been put on blood thinner medication for blood clots, and was visiting the Nation’s nursing station once a week for blood work.

She eventually became lethargic and “began to lose feeling in her fingers,” the backgrounder noted, and she ultimately died of a brain haemorrhage after being transported to Thunder Bay.

Brain haemorrhages are caused by a blood vessel leaking or bursting in the brain, essentially drowning it.

Prior to her death, on Aug. 19, Mamakwa had made a grim post on social media: “If I die, please go after them.”

On Friday, Falconer and Mamakwa’s parents, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, issued a statement announcing they had sent a formal request to Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner Thomas Carrique.

“The wanton and reckless disregard shown for Miranda’s health, and ultimately her life, by those public officials responsible for arranging her medical transportation makes such an investigation a necessity,” the statement said.

Eva and Mike are staying out of the public eye, but did comment in the statement.

“This should never have happened to Miranda. She should be alive today,” they said. “We deserve to know how something like this happened, and we want the individual or individuals responsible for failing to respond to these urgent requests for transportation to be held accountable. They cost Miranda her life. They cost her children a future without their mother.”

Mother of First Nations woman who couldn’t get medical transport and died seeks reform

Falconer said he does not take criminal cases lightly, but that this circumstance was “wonton neglect.”

“Three children are without a mother. A grandmother is left explaining to these children where their mother is. Words cannot describe the extent of the neglect here,” he said.

It’s also indicative of Canada’s failure to act in the best interests of Indigenous Peoples, he said.

Alongside this matter, the lawyer is also legal counsel to a coalition of several First Nations and tribal councils, led by Wunnumin Lake First Nation, Matawa Chiefs Council, and Windigo First Nations Council, which filed a human rights complaint against ISC on Oct. 1.

“The complaint alleges widespread neglect and systemic discrimination by the NIHB, whose routine administrative failures effectively deny life-sustaining healthcare to remote, fly-in communities,” stated a release on the Falconers legal practice’s website.

The coalition is seeking “sweeping structural overhauls,” as well as $20,000 in damages for those who missed medical appointments, and an additional $20,000 in “compensation for damages due to Canada’s willful and reckless conduct.”

Similar to Mamakwa’s case, members of Wummumin Lake, a fly-in community with no full-time doctor, “were subject to 147 missed medical appointments between March 2025 and March 2026 alone,” because of NIHB not arranging transportation, according to Falconer.

He said this would not happen in a place like Toronto.

“They are captive to the system that’s in place and the system is supposed to be in place to honour Treaty promises,” he said. “And we have benefited through privilege and wealth from these Treaties.

“Now what we’re seeing is basically a collapse of the medical responsibility that Canada bears. And what’s outrageous about all of this is that rest assured, if a failure of this kind happened to a white family, you can absolutely be assured there would be a criminal investigation.”

Internal review underway, stated ISC

According to a statement sent to APTN News, ISC has been in the process of “reviewing the circumstances of [Mamakwa’s] passing” since Sept. 11.

This was in part due to requests for an investigation from the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority (SLFNHA) and leadership from Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN), which represents 49 First Nations in Ontario, the statement read.

“A dedicated team has been established by ISC to conduct the review,” ISC spokesperson Carolane Gratton wrote. “Guided by an ISC Patient Safety facilitator, the team will conduct interviews and discussions to map relevant interactions and identify all contributing factors, both internal and external. The team will invite input from Ms. Mamakwa’s family and others involved in her circle of care as part of the review process and the development of recommendations.”

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty also met with NAN and SLFNHA on Sept. 30, and “continues to be in open dialogue while ISC provides support,” according to the statement.

Falconer said Gull-Masty has not been in touch with Mamakwa’s family, to his knowledge.

Falconer said a review is not enough, and the case needs “serious accountability.”

“If you know of and are implicated in the deprivation of essential health services to another human, and you are paid to provide those services, and you are implicated in denying those services, you should expect to get a knock on the door from the authorities. That’s certainly the country we live in for non-Indigenous people,” he said.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: ‘We take care of each other’: Voices from Montreal’s Cabot Square
content:
In Montreal’s Cabot Square, where homeless Indigenous people have gathered for decades, news that a member of the city’s police services (SPVM) had been suspended for urinating on homeless Montrealers was greeted largely without shock.




Regular visitors, as well as outreach workers from the various organizations serving unhoused populations in the west of downtown, describe relations between homeless people and police in and around Cabot Square as marked by distrust and fear.




People APTN News spoke with in Cabot Square over the last two weeks reported accumulating tickets, amounting to hundreds of dollars in fines, for fare evasion on the city’s transit system or jaywalking on Ste. Catherine Street. People who drink alcohol in the Square also said they’d received tickets for open containers. 

Few make any attempt to pay the tickets. For them, getting another ticket is simply a fact of life in Cabot Square, though one that may give police a reason to eventually arrest them.

Measuring one block by one block, Cabot Square is the only significant piece of greenspace in the western end of downtown Montreal. Located on Ste. Catherine St. at the corner of Atwater Ave., the Square is directly across from the former Montreal Forum.

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: What’s at stake for Indigenous Peoples in the U.S. as midterm elections draw near?
content:
On Tuesday, U.S. voters will cast their ballots in the country’s midterm elections. The elections come halfway through a president’s four year term.

A record-breaking number of Indigenous candidates–at least 355–are running in this year’s race.

This week on InFocus, Pawnee/Ponca lawyer Brett Chapman tells us about the candidates he’s following and how Native Americans are feeling the impact of Trump’s second term.

A recent study by the Brookings Institution reported that the Trump administration slashed $469 million in grants and contracts to tribal communities.

“I think a big problem with the administration, the second go around, is that because of the focus by them on DEI [Diversity, Equity and Inclusion], things of that nature, they have really tried to reduce Native American issues to [being] race-based,” Chapman said.

“What defines being Native American in the United States is not being a member of a race. It’s political sovereignty in the history of over 500 tribes having treaties with the government, and they’re having their own governments. And so you’re having a government-to-government relationship.

“You’re really seeing a weakening of that when it should be stronger.”

title: N.W.T. premier commits to advancing Dene control of child welfare
content:
Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson says the territorial government will begin discussions with Yellowknives Dene First Nations on formalizing their authority over child and family services, following concerns raised at the Annual Akaitcho Assembly about Indigenous children in care.




Speaking to delegates at the Chief Drygeese Centre on Oct. 28, Simpson said that while Indigenous governments already have the authority to care for their own children, the next step is to begin working toward a coordination agreement between governments under federal legislation.




“In terms of the child welfare piece, we will begin those conversations,” Simpson said. “It’s federal legislation, and it requires an implementation,” said Simpson.




The discussions come as delegates described children being separated from their siblings and communities, families struggling to access services and concerns about whether the child welfare system adequately reflects Indigenous cultures and ways of life.




According to a 2026 federal audit, 98 per cent of children who receive prevention and protection services in the N.W.T. are Indigenous, despite making up only about 58 per cent of the territory’s total child population.

author: Fraser Needham
title: Columnist says more pressing issues on agenda at First Nations meeting than abolishing Indian Act
content:
A columnist with the Hill Times says a First Nations meeting with First Ministers this week was not the appropriate venue to be discussing abolishing the more than a century-and-a-half old Indian Act.

“It seems to me that a lot of things were said at mics on that day that people really regret,” Rose LeMay said. “I don’t know anyone who would disagree that the Indian Act has to go. It’s a racist piece of segregationist law. It always has been. Whether we take out a clause here or there it’s still fundamentally a barrier to human rights. Especially for First Nations women. We’ve seen all the debate on S-2 and trying to bring in the one parent instead of the second-generation cut-off. Overall, it’s a piece of racist legislation. Was that day the day to raise it? I don’t think so.”

Lemay said it is her understanding that much more time in the meeting was spent on discussing how the government’s proposed Bill C-39 – the Building Canada Strong Act – could affect First Nations rights when it comes resource development.

She also said more pressing issues including First Nations access to health care and systemic discrimination against First Nations women should have been given more of a focus by government ministers in post meeting media scrums.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Federal government says lack of housing on First Nations ‘strictly’ a funding issue
content:
During the final hour of a two-day hearing at the Federal Court of Appeal, lawyers representing First Nations and Canada argued whether the matter of water and housing on reserve land was about money or human rights.

Canada asserted that when it comes to providing housing, the government “is limited” to providing funding for the homes, making the issue a matter of financial duty.

“First Nations manage their own housing,” said one of Canada’s lawyers. “Leadership determines what is to be built, where it is to be built, and how it will be contained.”

However, lawyers representing Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point First Nations asked how that could be possible, when the Indian Act had caused the housing shortages that are affecting Indigenous communities in the first place.

“There’s such extreme harm that we can say that there’s no way a First Nation would have brought this on itself if it could have afforded it,” said Michael Rosenberg, one of an equally plentiful team of lawyers representing the Nations.

The federal government had recently appealed two decisions made by Federal Court Justice Paul Favel in December 2025, when he had concluded that Canada had the obligation to provide Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point First Nations access to housing and clean drinking water.

“The lawsuit at its heart is about funding and increased funding, not an abstract separation of right,” said a lawyer representing the Liberal government on Wednesday.

Over a phone call, Rosenberg also confirmed to APTN News that, in alignment with that claim, the government was also asking for court costs alongside the appeals.

Back in court, he said the communities were not able to properly provide for themselves without financial and structural support from the government, and Canada did, in fact, still have control over all of the houses on a reserve.

“Part of what has kept these First Nations in this state [of poor housing] has been Canada’s part in the Indian Act, constructed to deprive them,” he said.

Rosenberg argued that according to a report from the Auditor General of Canada submitted to Parliament in 2024, Canada was still in the process of transferring control of housing back to the First Nations.

In the report he referenced that the auditor general had also concluded that, “We found that Indigenous Services Canada was at the early stages of transferring control of housing to First Nations, but no overarching policy framework was in place to guide the department’s work in transferring its programs to First Nations communities.

“Under the Department of Indigenous Services Act,” the report continued, “Indigenous Services Canada is mandated to work with First Nations to gradually transfer departmental responsibilities to First Nations, including housing. As of 31 March 2023, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation did not have the legislative mandate to transfer its responsibilities to First Nations.”

The report also stated that this transfer process “is not imposed” on the First Nations, and they need to want to take over those responsibilities.

Rosenberg said many communities have not expressed that interest because they “aren’t able to provide that support,” without money from Canada.

He said, according to evidence from the original lawsuit, the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) even “resisted the idea of moving Canada’s commitment to First Nations,” which he described as “divesting itself [Canada] of its own commitment.”

Instead, the AFN, a political organization that represents more than 600 First Nations in Canada, has been developing a National First Nations Housing and Infrastructure Strategy, which is a lengthy transition period done in collaboration with ISC, since 2018.

The proposed strategy would include transferring control of funding as well.

“The success of any recognition of First Nations complete authority over their housing depends on a federal initiative to transfer control of housing programs and services funds that is broadly flexible enough to accommodate the wide range of First Nations preferences,” the national organization stated in a release.

This is in part due to “circular funding,” he said, as the government will fund housing projects that require rent, and the rent then paid to the government by members will be dollars collected from government checks.

“That is the dynamic here, however it is dressed up,” he said.

As of 2025, the AFN was still “urging the federal government to honour its intent to transfer control of the First Nations Housing Market Fund (the Fund) to First Nations control,” in order to properly assume control over housing as a whole.

Although Canada has retained that funding, lawyers representing the government said housing is otherwise out of their hands.

“Canada does not dispute the importance of housing, which is why [it] has put billions of dollars towards funding on reserve,” one of its lawyers said. “My friend’s submissions today leave this Court with the impression that the record suggests that Canada does, in fact say who can build, what can build, but respectfully that is not the case.”

The lawyer said “There is a shared responsibility … Not simply the system which Canada determines, it’s a framework that involves consultation at a policy level.”

The three Federal Justices have yet to make a determination.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon photographer captures caribou’s extraordinary fight for survival
content:
It’s an incredible act of nature.




Two caribou. Their antlers locked in battle. One dead. The survivor, nearly immobilized by the weight of his opponent, preyed upon by a bear as foxes and birds scavenge the dead bull’s remains.




Yukon

 photographer 

Peter Mather

 captured the remarkable images earlier this month while filming the Southern Lakes caribou’s rut, when up to a few hundred animals gather and males spar for females.




“I have never seen anything like that before,” Mather said. “Their horns are locked together, and one of them is dead. And the bear is like sitting 10 feet away, just watching, trying to figure out what to do. It was the strangest situation.”




Mather came across the rare sighting about 20 kilometres south of Whitehorse while filming content for the Kwanlin Dün First Nation as part of a project for the Southern Lakes Caribou Steering Committee. Kwanlin Dün is one of six First Nations governments represented on the committee.




With fewer than 1,000 animals in the early 1990s, the Southern Lakes caribou, which is composed of four woodland herds, has increased to about 4,000 today, thanks in part to voluntary harvest moratoriums by First Nations.

title: First Nations youth, MP Leah Gazan warn new federal laws threaten rights, water and consent
content:
First Nations youth and NDP Indigenous affairs critic Leah Gazan used a Parliament Hill news conference Wednesday to warn that three major federal bills risk undermining treaty rights, free, prior and informed consent, and protections for water and land.




Gazan was joined by Ramon Kataquapit, who sits on the 

Chiefs of Ontario’s Youth Council

, and other First Nations youth advocates, Jeronimo Kataquapit, Cedar Iahtail, Dara Wawatie-Chabot, Katisha Paul and Celine Debassige. 




They focused on the proposed bills, C-39 (the Building Canada Strong Act), C-37 (the First Nations Clean Water Act), and the Bill C-5, which passed in 2025, arguing the legislation prioritizes rapid resource development over Indigenous jurisdiction and long-term community health.




Gazan said that Bill C-39’s one-year review timelines and expanded ministerial powers to exempt projects from certain environmental and heritage rules effectively hinder Section 35 rights and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Federal drinking water lawsuit ‘not a case of government spending,’ says lawyer
content:
A lawyer representing Shamattawa First Nation says that if Canada is in control of what’s being built on reserve land, then it would also be responsible for addressing the needs related to clean drinking water and housing.

“If you don’t take Canada’s money, the infrastructure does not get built, does not get operated, does not get maintained,” said defense lawyer Michael Rosenburg, during a hearing in the Federal Court of Appeal on Wednesday in Winnipeg. “That is the dynamic, because these First Nations have been put in this position of dependence.”

In December 2025, Federal Court Justice Paul Favel determined that, in his rulings for two separate class-action lawsuits from Shamattawa and St. Theresa First Nations, that Canada had the obligation to provide these communities with access to housing and clean drinking water.

In one of the decisions, Favel said that the federal government “exerted direct control over every facet of First Nations life through legislations, regulations, policies, and practices since at least the 1880s,” and that “this extends to matters such as water infrastructure.”

However, Canada had appealed that decision, arguing that the lawsuit is based on policy and funding issues rather than a legally binding duty.

During the first of a two-day hearing, a team of lawyers representing the federal government argued that because First Nations are self-governed, they would then be responsible for their own water treatment. Additionally, because Canada was not responsible for the water itself, the 2025 lawsuits were based on funding for infrastructure, which Canada has provided.

Therefore, the government would have no obligation to solve the problems themselves.

The government also argued that Favel had referred to previous cases when making his determination, which had concerned restrictions or decisions that would have interfered with people’s access to resources such as drinking water, “which left open the possibility that a positive obligation could exist, but did not go as far as recognize the general duty.”

Canada’s lawyers called the obligation an “assertion,” which they said Favel backed with no new evidence beyond historical issues such as the impact of colonialism on First Nations, which face these barriers.

Another argument made by Canada was that experts used in the original cases were not reliable.

An example of this claim was Lawrence Reynolds, a retired doctor who had been consulted on the subject of drinking water, who had been “expressly and improperly charged with determining Canada had control over water.”

This was because “water is not fixed and immovable; water migrates, it moves from place to place,” a lawyer said.

Canada also pointed to the Constitution Act, which, according to section 35, “recognizes and affirms the existing Aboriginal and treaty rights of the Aboriginal peoples of Canada,” including the right to “responsibly spend funds,” lawyers said, meaning money which would be allocated to repairing water treatment plants on traditional land.

Rosenburg said making the case about funding undermines the human rights concerns brought up by the communities in the original lawsuits.

“When you exercise such close control, it does not allow Canada to say that when something goes wrong, First Nations have full responsibility,” he said, adding that Canada has full control over infrastructure on First Nations, down to the “colour of the pipes.”

“Class members are between a rock and hard place because the defendant put them there,” he said.

Rosenburg said that Favel had written about the “core of the relationship” between First Nations peoples and Canada, which is “creating a systemic disadvantage by confining them to remote and economic reserves where they’re dependent on Canada to make those lands livable,” and then “imposing restrictions on what they can do to live on reserve from both a regulatory and a fiscal perspective.”

He said this is what would separate the case from “ordinary government spending.”

“You heard my friends reference self-governance, the importance of ensuring that First Nations can govern their own affairs. But that cannot be an excuse to tell First Nations that they must make ends meet when they’re still subject to this [relationship] and they haven’t been restored to a position where they have the resources and the control to make their reserve livable.

“Now ultimately, Canada’s role in creating and maintaining class members’ disadvantage will be critical to delineating the extent of the federal government’s obligations. Recognized class members do not call for unlimited government liability. They do not call for guaranteed outcomes. What they ask is the care to make reasonable efforts to assist to the extent that it is responsible for their inability to realize the promise of a reserve as a livable homeland.”

According to the Indigenous Services website, there are 39 drinking water advisories in Canada from Newfoundland and Labrador to Alberta. The majority of them are in Ontario, where another lawsuit was launched against the federal government. Six of them are in Manitoba.

In 2015, the Liberal government promised to end all water advisories.

The court is scheduled to resume Thursday morning.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Youths tell trial of climate change toll, from anxiety to flood and heat impacts
content:
Sadie Vipond says she was just seven years old when she began noticing the impacts of climate change.




Now a 20-year-old plaintiff in Canada’s first youth-led climate trial, Vipond described experiencing catastrophic floods in Calgary in 2013 that the city says resulted in mass evacuations, one death and $6 billion in financial losses.




“I was beginning to see different actions in my community around the climate crisis, and so I was also feeling very anxious about my future,” she told the Federal Court in Vancouver.




Vipond is one of 15 plaintiffs who are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.




The trial that began Monday heard in an opening statement from the youths’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”




She said the Charter must protect youth from their own government’s actions.




Vipond told the court on Tuesday that she had experienced several climate change events since the floods, including wildfire smoke and intense heat.




“I’ve been seeing these impacts all my life, and I’ve been seeing how these impacts are getting worse,” she said, adding that they had taken a toll on her mental health.

author: Karyn Pugliese
title: Nearly 200 First Nations leaders, the prime minister and premiers gathered for a historic meeting about almost everything. Now what?
content:
The John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive was perhaps, in its own imperfect way, a fitting place for nearly 200 First Nations leaders, most of the country’s premiers and a prime minister to hold a meeting First Nations have wanted for more than a century.




It’s actually two buildings mashed together: a modern glass construction, like a church nave, that lets light pour in from above and gives the hallways a sense of something sacred, while behind it, the old city hall rises as a plain grey slab, a maze of stairs leading to small, dark meeting rooms. 




Outside, the chief set up teepees that strangely echo the building’s peaks.




Three very different structures, sharing the same address.




“This is the first time in 119 years of Crown-First Nations relations that a first ministers meeting has focused solely on First Nations,” Cindy Woodhouse-Nepinak, the national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has said many times leading up to the meeting and it’s a line she would repeat at the gathering.




Of course, a hundred-year wait puts a lot of pressure on a meeting.

title: Cowichan Tribes to propose solution protecting private property in January: lawyer
content:
The lawyer for the Cowichan Tribes said they will make a proposal in January that protects private property rights in the landmark Aboriginal title case that the B.C. Conservatives have said calls into question who controls British Columbia.




Lawyer David Rosenberg said that if it has “the right attitude,” the incoming Conservative government will find it easier to resolve the Cowichan case than to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, known as 

DRIPA

.




The 2025 Cowichan ruling on a portion of Crown, city and private land in Richmond, B.C., found that Aboriginal title is a “senior interest” compared with fee-simple title, and sections of B.C.’s Land Title Act that establish fee-simple title as “indefeasible” do not apply to Aboriginal title.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Canada appeals landmark rulings that found it has legal duties on First Nations water and housing
content:
Chiefs from Shamattawa, St. Theresa Point and Sandy Lake First Nations return to court this week to defend landmark Federal Court decisions that recognized Canada’s legal duties to provide safe drinking water and adequate housing on reserve — rulings the Carney government is appealing.

“The Government of Canada continues to fight us in Court over one of our most basic rights as human beings,” said Chief Jordna Hill of Shamattawa First Nation. “But Canada knows what it has done to First Nations people is wrong.”

“Canada ships bottled water to reserves for their federal employees, while First Nations people living under long-term drinking water advisories are forced to use the contaminated tap water.”

The two court cases in question that the Federal Government is appealing are Shamattawa First Nation v. Canada [Water] and St. Theresa Point First Nation v. Canada [Housing].

The federal government is appealing two decisions released in December 2025 by Federal Court Justice Paul Favel. In those decisions, he ruled that Canada owes fiduciary duties, a common law duty of care, and Charter rights to equality, life, liberty and security of the person, and religion in relation to on-reserve drinking water and housing.

According to the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs, Canada continues to argue it has no legally enforceable obligations, attributes difficulties on reserves to First Nations themselves, and is seeking costs against the First Nations.

Chief Elvin Flett of St. Theresa Point Anisininew Nation said the federal government created and reinforced the housing crisis.

“The federal government put First Nations in an impossible position by creating and reinforcing our housing crisis. We are now living in a permanent state of emergency. We have had no choice but to turn to the courts for our survival,” he said.

“While we would have preferred to work with Canada as nation-to-nation partners, Canada has made clear that we will need to enforce our rights through the courts for anything to change.”

According to the Assembly of Manitoba’s Chiefs Favel’s water decision ran 59 pages. and rested on roughly 10,000 pages of evidence.

The housing decision was 122 pages and drew on about 12,000 pages.

The court found that many members live on reserves that are isolated and “lack a viable economic base,” making commercial and residential development impractical. In those circumstances, the judge wrote, Canada can either provide the resources needed or restore First Nations to a position where they can provide for themselves, but it cannot maintain the status quo.

The court also rejected Canada’s attempt to ignore the legacy of colonial policies and the Indian Act, which has controlled nearly every aspect of life on reserve.

Favel found that a structural deficit has left many First Nations unable to keep up with housing needs since the creation of reserves.

Chief Delores Kakegamic of Sandy Lake First Nation said the conditions would be treated as a political crisis anywhere else.

“For too long Canada has swept the housing crisis on reserves under the rug. Canada’s politicians and bureaucrats have been satisfied with doing the bare minimum while First Nation members were forced to live in decrepit and overcrowded homes that harm their health, safety, and community,” she said.

“If these on-reserve housing conditions existed elsewhere, it would be a political crisis.”

Grand Chief Kyra Wilson of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs linked the appeals to the language of partnership heard at this week’s First Nations–First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa.

“At the First Nations–First Ministers Meeting, Canada spoke of partnership. This week, it will stand in a Winnipeg courtroom and argue it owes First Nations no duty to provide safe drinking water or adequate housing. Canada cannot have it both ways,” Wilson said. “Instead of spending undisclosed sums on lawyers to fight Shamattawa and St. Theresa Point, Canada should honour its Treaty obligations and put that money into water plants and homes.”

Court confirms Canada is liable for water and housing woes

The December 2025 decisions by Favel are the first contested rulings to hold that Canada owes First Nations legally enforceable duties to provide reliable access to safe drinking water on reserve and adequate housing on remote reserves.

The federal government has tabled the First Nations Clean Water Act while simultaneously arguing in court against it.

Until these judgments, the federal government largely treated water and housing on reserve as policy or funding questions rather than judicious legal obligations.

If the Federal Courts of Appeal upholds the decisions, First Nations gain a stronger judicial tool to compel action and remedies instead of relying solely on political commitments or discretionary funding programs.

The Federal Court of Appeal will hear the cases on Oct. 28 and 29. The case will also be livestreamed.

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Treaty One opens campus to the first national First Nations business training centre
content:
The CEO of a First Nations-led centre for business education and mentorship says that her goal is to shift the narrative so that Indigenous Peoples are not seen as “recipients,” but “creators and innovators” of wealth and services.

Kathleen Bluesky leads the Wiitahnookiinitaw Tahshkayzing Entrepreneurship Centre (WTEC), which is, according to its website, “Canada’s first fully First Nations-led Business Incubator.”

WTEC was founded in May 2025, but did not have a physical location until Tuesday.

“When we talk about First Nations economic development, it usually starts with what we lack,” Bluesky said at the grand opening event. “We lack capital, we lack capacity, we lack opportunities. And those barriers are real, I’m not trying to deny that, and we do have to address them, but I believe the conversation has to start with, what do our people already bring?

“We bring knowledge, we bring our relationships, and we bring our determination, and we show up,” she continued. “And we’ve been providing for our people, our families, our communities, for generations, and we will continue to do so.”

She said, “aside from the paint on the walls,” the space, located on the third floor of 191 Broadway St. in downtown Winnipeg, was funded entirely by First Nations startups who have benefited from services at WTEC since its inception.

“So I’m very proud of that,” she said.

The centre was developed by Treaty One Development Corporation (T1DC) “in collaboration with Treaty One Nations and key development partners,” according to its website, which includes a partnership with the province of Manitoba.

Treaty One is composed of seven First Nations in Manitoba, and T1DC is the economic and business stream that retains control from leadership.

WTEC to support planned business district through training youth, says CEO

Under Treaty One leadership, WTEC will also play a part in what the National Indigenous Economic Development Board has labeled “the largest urban reserve in Canada” — Naawi-Oodena, which is 108 acres and located within Winnipeg.

The 2021 Naawi-Oodena Master Plan, developed by T1DC, proposed a mixed-use village, high-and-low density residential neighbourhoods, a business district, schools and community spaces, and more, to be slowly built over several years.

The first completed project was the Oodena Gas and Convenience Store, which opened to the public in June 2025.

Additionally, on March 18, the federal government announced that its Housing Accelerator Fund would support a $91 million apartment block project, with additional funds from the province.

With a predicted completion in January 2028, the project — which “requires a minimum 30 per cent Indigenous workforce, with 20 per cent consisting of Treaty One First Nation members,” according to the government release — would allow for Naawi-Oodena’s first 260 housing units on-site.

With housing underway, WTEC will contribute to the business district, Bluesky said.

“What I want to see is more First Nation businesses winning major contracts, more First Nations women building enterprises, more young people being on the entrepreneurial path, and more of our businesses growing from community operations into regional, national and international companies with wealth staying in communities,” she said. “That’s what I want to see.”

Alongside its mentorship program, WTEC offers a “three-month boot camp and business feasibility analysis certificate” called Roots to Rise, as well as a certificate program in partnership with the Western British Columbia Polytechnic College (WBCPC), according to its website.

Bluesky said that currently, there are about 30 entrepreneurs enrolled in WTEC programs, and she’s happy they now have a space to study and speak with mentors.

“We’re not starting from nothing, we’re building on everything that came before us,” Bluesky said, “and I want our entrepreneurs to know that you belong here. Your ideals, and your language and your culture belong here.”

Premier Wab Kinew, who was present at the location’s grand opening, said his provincial government was “very, very happy to support this.

“I just think it’s really important to have entrepreneurship,” he said. “There’s so much uncertainty in the world today …The best way to have certainty in a time of uncertainty is to make your own destiny. And that includes making your own destiny when it comes to what you do for a living.

“You look at the mentors for the entrepreneurs, and it’s a real who’s-who for Winnipeg’s business community, so let’s work together and get this next generation on a good footing.”

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

title: First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun says it’s up to citizens to decide how to move forward on Eagle mine
content:
The First Nation at the centre of the Eagle gold mine disaster in north-central Yukon says it will ultimately be up to its citizens to decide how it plans to support the sale of the mine to a foreign mining company.

The First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun, on whose traditional territory the mine is located, indicated in an Oct. 23 news release that while negotiations with Singapore-based mining and acquisitions company Boroo are in the early stages, the relationship appears positive.

“Boroo has approached our Nation with openness, respect and good faith, and we recognize the positive foundation that has been established,” it says.

“We are not turning away from mining. We believe the answer is to do it better,” it adds.

The release says the First Nation is not granting any interviews for the time being.

A failure at the mine’s heap leach facility in June 2024 saw more than 300,000 cubic metres of cyanide-contaminated water released into the surrounding environment on the First Nation’s traditional territory. The mine subsequently went into receivership.

The Yukon government and PricewaterhouseCoopers, the mine’s receiver, announced last week that they had reached an agreement to sell the mine for up to $140 million, a process they said will include input from Na-Cho Nyäk Dun.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Former CEO sues Métis Nation-Saskatchewan, secretariat
content:
Richard Quintal, the former CEO of the Métis Nation-Saskatchewan (MN-S) is suing the organization for wrongful dismissal and breaching his employment contract. Quintal was let go in the spring of 2026.

According to the statement of claim filed Sept. 21 in the Court of King’s Bench in Saskatoon, Quintal is also alleging bad-faith conduct in the way he was dismissed, including the public termination, reversal, suspension, and subsequent investigations the claim alleges were intended to help MN-S avoid its contractual severance obligation.

“The Plaintiff states that the Defendants failed to uphold the obligation of good faith and fair dealing in the manner of dismissal, particularly with respect to the public without cause termination of the Plaintiff…,” the claim alleges.

At the heart of Quintal’s claim is the terms of his employment contract with MN-S.

“The Plaintiff commenced employment with the Defendants on January 8, 2018, through the federal government Interchange Program. The Plaintiff was then offered employment by the Defendants as MNS’s Chief of Staff through a fixed-term contract of employment dated July 20, 2019,” the claim says.

“The contract was then replaced and superseded by a fixed-term extension contract dated December 1, 2022, which, among other things, appointed the Plaintiff Chief of Staff/Chief Executive Officer of MNS, and extended the Plaintiff’s employment with the Defendants to November 30, 2027.”

The claim goes on to allege that “this extension contract was further amended by the Defendants on or about May 9, 2024, and included an extension of the Plaintiff’s employment with the Defendants to July 31, 2030.”

The statement of claim says “significantly, the Contract stated the employment relationship may be terminated without cause upon the Defendants’ providing the Plaintiff with a lump-sum payment…”

According to the claim, the payment is to be equal to whichever is greater: “the minimum notice or pay in lieu of notice and severance pay,” or “the remainder of the Annual Base Salary which would have been payable over the term of the Agreement if the Plaintiff’s employment had not been terminated…”

Quintal is also seeking aggravated or moral damages, punitive damages, special damages, interest, legal costs, and “any further relief the court permits,” according to the claim.

Quintal alleges in the claim he received a letter dated May 13, explaining he was being placed on paid administrative leave while a review was conducted “into the circumstances that led to the extension of his contract to July 2030.”

“The letter stated that the PMC was not aware of (Quintal’s)Contract extension. This claim was made in spite of the fact that at least three members of the PMC at the time…” President Glen McCallum, Marg Friesen, and Brennan Merasty had “full knowledge of the Contract extension at the time the Contract was amended and were in communication regarding the said extension,” Quintal’s claim alleges.

Allegations and accusations dogged Quintal as far back as 2020, according to reports in the media.

Quintal claims he experienced bullying and harassment by certain Provincial Métis Council (PMC) members, and was “publicly discredited and humiliated.”

Several members of MN-S were “suspended pending an apology to the Plaintiff,” however a negotiated resolution followed in April 2025.

The elected members were invited to rejoin the PMC and the Métis Nation Legislative Assembly (MNLA) on May 20, 2026.

“We’ve pushed the reset button to be able to start a new journey…[so]that the obligations of your government [are] not put on the sidelines,” President Glen McCallum said at the time.

The MN-S also lifted the bans against 12 Métis citizens who also had received cease and desist letters last fall.

In a letter sent to the citizens in April, 2026, the Nation’s legal counsel said the rescinding of the letters is not an admission of “liability or wrongdoing by MN-S or the PMC.”

According to Quintal’s statement of claim, he says MNS advised him on April 23 that it would terminate him without cause. The Provincial Métis Council then passed a resolution making the termination effective May 15, publicly announced the change, and began planning a transition.

Quintal alleges in the claim that after he cooperated with the transition, MNS allegedly rescinded the termination decision on May 11, placed him on paid administrative leave, and said it would review how his contract had been extended to 2030.

Quintal further alleges that senior officials knew about the extension when it was made, contrary to the stated reason for the review.

MN-S’s counsel later confirmed his termination effective June 11, 2026, while reserving the right to rely on “after-acquired cause.” Investigations were commenced into the contract extension, a separation agreement involving another employee, bonus payments, and executive health benefits.

The allegations in Quintal’s statement of claim have not been proven in court.

The MN-S filed a notice of intent on Oct. 14 that it planned to make a statement of defense and has been granted an extension do so to Nov. 30, 2026 according to the court file.

APTN News reached out to the MN-S for comment but were advised by MN–S media relations manager, Rena Montgomerie that “because the matter is before the courts, MN–S will have no comment.”

title: 72 ans après sa mort, la dépouille du bébé Maxime retourne à Manawan
content:
Après un moment pour reprendre son souffle, Manon Ottawa s’exprime devant les médias. « Aujourd’hui, je suis profondément émue de pouvoir annoncer officiellement la date de son retour. »

Elle fait référence au retour de la dépouille de son oncle Maxime. Soixante-douze ans après sa mort, presqu’au jour le jour, le bébé Maxime revient enfin parmi les siens. « Bébé Maxime reviendra à Manawan, sur la terre de nos ancêtres, auprès de sa famille et de son peuple atikamekw. »

C’est un témoignage parmi tant d’autres de l’histoire des enfants autochtones disparus. À l’âge de six mois, bébé Maxime a dû être transporter en hydro-avion à l’hôpital de La Tuque. Seul. « Imaginer la douleur d’une mère qui voit partir son enfant sans pouvoir l’accompagner », dit Manon. Il a ensuite été transféré vers l’hôpital de Québec sans qu’on en avise ses parents. Après 43 jours à l’hôpital, bébé Maxime est mort le 5 octobre 1954.

Conférence de presse du 22 octobre, 2026.

Lors de la conférence de presse, l’avocate de la famille Ottawa, Olivia Malenfant, continue à raconter l’histoire du bébé Maxime : « Ses parents n’apprennent de son décès que 2 ans plus tard. Pendant tout ce temps, ils ignorent ce qui est advenu de leur enfant. Ils ne peuvent ni lui dire adieu, ni lui offrir des funérailles, ni lui offrir une sépulture conforme à leurs traditions. Pendant des décennies, la famille est demeurée sans réponses qu’en aux circonstances du décès de bébé Maxime et l’endroit où il a été inhumé. Cette absence d’information concernant le sort d’un proche, la plupart du temps un enfant, est une réalité à laquelle de nombreuses familles autochtones ont été confrontés. »

En 2014, pour honorer la dernière volonté de son père, Manon Ottawa a entrepris les recherches pour retrouver son oncle – le bébé maxime. « Ce parcours n’a pas été facile. Il y a eu des obstacles, des moments de découragement, des longues attentes et beaucoup d’émotions. Mais je n’ai jamais abandonné. »

En octobre 2025, la cour supérieure du Québec accepte une exhumation d’un lot où se trouvaient 5 personnes au total. Maître Malenfant explique que l’exhumation fût complexe, non seulement à cause du nombre de personnes dans le lot creusé, mais aussi parce que « les lots adjacents complétaient 4 défunts d’un côté et 5 de l’autre. Toutes des personnes autochtones. »

À ce moment, un corps présumé d’être celui du bébé Maxime a été envoyé pour identification au Laboratoire de sciences judiciaires et de médecine légale. « Des analyses et des tests d’ADN ont ensuite été effectués afin de confirmer son identité. Le 30 septembre 2026, lors de la Journée nationale de la vérité et de la réconciliation, nous avons reçu la confirmation tant attendue. Les résultats étaient concluants », précise Manon. « Je ne m’attendais pas à ça. J’ai pleuré parce que c’était un soulagement. »

Manon a pris un instant pour « remercier sincèrement le Conseil des Atikamekw de Manawan, ainsi que l’association Awacak, Petits êtres de lumière. » Constant Awashish, Grand chef du Conseil de la nation Atikamekw était présent. « La famille, finalement, avoir des réponses à leurs questionnements qui a duré 72 ans quand même. C’est long. Il y a des gens qui sont décédés, des membres de la famille qui sont décédés au courant des années, sans savoir qu’est-ce qui était passé avec bébé maxime. Puis aujourd’hui, je pense que c’est grâce au travail acharné de l’équipe à Awacak, de la communauté, de la famille qui n’ont pas abandonné leur recherche. On peut trouver un dénouement à toute cette période sombre qui a pu affecter de la famille. »

Cette démarche, affirme Manon, est devenue beaucoup plus grande que leur seule histoire familiale. « En cherchant bébé maxime, d’autres enfants ont également été retrouvé. » Le grand chef Awashish précise que « le chemin est tracé. C’est parmi les premiers qui ont réussi à faire l’exercice. Je sais qu’il y en a d’autres dans la Nation atikamekw qui recherchent des membres de leur famille, en espérant que ça peut apporter de l’espoir et de l’encouragement. »

Photo d’archives. 16 décembre, 2019 : une des premières rencontres d’APTN avec Manon Ottawa, où elle nous montre le tikinan.

Sur la table de la conférence de presse, un tikinan décoré. Le même type de porte-bébé dans lequel ses grands-parents avaient déposé le petit Maxime lors de son départ vers l’hôpital. Manon l’avait acheté au début de ses recherche, se promettant que tant que bébé maxime ne serait trouvé, cela resterait un objet sans nom. Maintenant, Manon peut fièrement dire que c’est un porte-bébé. Un qui porte une histoire. « Je vais le garder pour pouvoir le garder auprès de moi. Pour que jamais personne ne puisse vivre ce que ma grand-mère a vécu. »

Bébé maxime retournera parmi les siens à Manawan le 26 octobre, afin d’être réinhumer le 28 octobre – jour d’anniversaire du père à Manon. Un beau cadeau. « Il m’aurait dit qu’il a demandé à la bonne personne pour pouvoir retrouver son petit frère. », dit Manon en riant.

Une boucle se ferme pour la famille Ottawa. Et un nom – celui de Maxime – sera maintenant toujours porteur d’espoir. « Ma fille a appelé son enfant maxime. Il va y avoir beaucoup d’autres Maximes qui vont naître. »

author: The Canadian Press
title: Atikamekw baby to be reburied in home community more than 70 years after death
content:
More than 70 years after his death, an Atikamekw baby buried far from his family in Quebec City will be laid to rest in his home community.




After 12 years of searching, the family of Maxime Ottawa has located his burial site, exhumed his remains and confirmed his identity, bringing what relatives describe as “immense relief.”




“On Oct. 26, 2026, Baby Maxime will finally come home to Manawan, to his mother and father, to his brothers and sisters,” his niece, Manon Ottawa, said Thursday at a news conference in Montreal.




Maxime was the brother of her father, Henri Ottawa, whose wish to find out what happened to the child prompted her to begin searching in 2014.




Manawan is an Atikamekw community located about 250 kilometres north of Montreal.




In 1954, when Maxime was just six months old, he was taken from Manawan to La Tuque, Que., for medical treatment without his parents.




He was later transferred to Quebec City without his family being informed. He died on Oct. 5, 1954, after 43 days in the hospital, without his loved ones having the chance to see him one last time.




His parents only learned of his death two years later and were unable to hold a funeral or bury him according to their traditions and beliefs.




“In 2014, four years after the death of my father Henri, I began searching, according to his wishes, to find my uncle,” Ottawa told reporters.

title: ITK president hopes we’ve learned from the past as the world’s interests turn to Inuit Nunangat
content:
While Natan Obed says this will be his last term as president of 

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

 (ITK), he says there is still a lot of unfinished business and big things on the horizon.




As an example, Obed, who is into his 11th year leading the ITK, the national organization representing Inuit interests in Canada, says “it seems like the world’s interests are descending upon our homeland.”




“Strategically, Inuit Nunangat is at the forefront of global considerations,” says Obed, referring to the traditional and contemporary homeland of Inuit in Canada.




“The defense and security of this country and the territorial integrity of this country is at stake,” says Obed on the latest episode of Face to Face.




The federal government has announced more over $30 billion in funding for military and defense in Inuit Nunangat. The investments would go towards airfields, hangars and other facilities in Yellowknife and Inuvik, N.W.T.,  Iqaluit, Nunavut and Goose Bay, Labrador.




Operational hubs and bases have also been announced for Resolute, Cambridge Bay and Rankin Inlet in Nunavut.




For Obed, the interest in Inuit Nunangat is reminiscent of what happened during the Second World War and Cold War.




“Over the next 15 to 20 years, then there were installations that were built all across the Canadian Arctic and that forever transformed the lives of Canadian Inuit,” says Obed.

Band members from nations throughout Alberta turned out in droves to cast their ballots in an attempt to stop a potential binding future referendum on the province separating from Canada. Some unofficial reports on social media claimed First Nations turnout was three times higher than in any other election.




APTN News visited several polling places Monday where parking lots were filled with cars and lineups could still be seen out the doors shortly before polls closed at 8 p.m.

content:
After a months-long litigation,

The company announced it had received the loan Tuesday in a news release.




The Oakville, Ont.,-based Baffinland Iron Mines Corp., which operates the mine on northern Baffin Island, announced in May it had filed for creditor protection.




The $660-million loan from Export Development Canada, a Crown corporation, is intended to provide “liquidity” to keep the mine operational, said Celeste van Tonder, the company’s chief financial officer, in a sworn affidavit.




At the time, van Tonder said if Baffinland didn’t get the loan, the mine would be “forced to curtail or cease operations entirely and a significant number of employees may need to be placed on leave.”




Baffinland is Nunavut’s largest private-sector employer with approximately 1,200 people, including 300 Inuit employees.




The company will use the money for “operating costs, exploration and expansion,” said Ashley Glen, director at Export Development Canada, in a sworn affidavit on June 19.




There are limitations on how the company can spend the money.




The new agreement doesn’t allow Baffinland “excessive” spending on mining exploration or expansion, Glen said, defining these amounts as more than $14 million on exploration or over $28 million on expansion.

From community rallies in Maskwacis to an outcry over cancelled advance polling in Fort Chipewyan, Alberta’s separation referendum has brought First Nations leaders and grassroots organizers together across Treaty 6, 7 and 8.

title: Treaty rights and voting access at centre of Alberta referendum
content:
As Albertans prepare to vote on the province’s future in Canada, Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot says the separation debate raises questions about who would honour First Nations treaties and protect the rights they guarantee.




“There’s too many unanswered questions and there’s been no consultation with First Nations, and that’s a requirement as protected by the Constitution.” Crowfoot said.




Crowfoot’s great-great-great-grandfather, chief Crowfoot, was an original signatory of Treaty 7, which established a relationship between the Blackfoot people and the Crown. That treaty predates Alberta’s entry into Confederation in 1905.




The Oct. 19 referendum will ask Albertans whether the province should begin the process of separating from Canada. For First Nations, the question extends beyond provincial politics to treaty obligations, sovereignty and the Crown’s responsibility to uphold agreements protected by the Constitution.

title: Indigenous youth stuck in ‘revolving door’ of justice system: StatsCan
content:
A new report from Statistics Canada says Indigenous youth are stuck in a “revolving door” when it comes to repeat offences, which is perpetrated by factors ranging from unrealistic bail restrictions to over-policing.




The paper, published Thursday, also said that the overrepresentation of Indigenous Peoples in the Justice system extends to those younger than 18 and that there were measurable differences when it came to sentencing outcomes in cases involving Indigenous youth versus their white counterparts.




Data was collected between 2016/2017 and 2022/2023. Within that seven-year gap, First Nations, Métis, and Inuit defendants made up approximately 27 per cent of the youth court population, despite only forming eight per cent of minors in Canada overall.




On the other hand, the report found white youth were underrepresented, accounting for only 52 per cent of defendants despite making up 60 per cent of the youth population.




The imbalance was the most prominent in British Columbia and the northern territories, where Indigenous youth accounted for 43 per cent of the youth court population, nearly four times higher than what they make up of the total youth population in that entire region, which is 12 per cent.

content:

The resolution referred to water as “a sacred gift from the Creator” and called for greater Dene-led oversight of water quality, industrial activity and contamination across the North.




The conversation led by Gerry Cheezie, co-chair of Keepers of the Water and a former chief of the Tthebatthie Denesųłiné Nation, comes as Indigenous leaders raise concerns about proposed plans to treat and release oilsands tailings water into the Athabasca River, which flows north into the Mackenzie River basin.




The resolution states that Dene waters are facing increasing pressures from industrial development, resource extraction, climate change, contamination and cumulative effects.




Cheezie, who recently attended Suncor Energy Inc.’s engagement sessions on its plans to treat and release tailings, said the water issue has never been more urgent.




”We’re impacted and we don’t want to see our waters polluted,” Cheezie said.

title: Supreme Court decision balances Gladue factors against concern for Indigenous women
content:
The Supreme Court of Canada upheld a reduced sentence in the case of a Mi’kmaw man convicted of brutally assaulting his Mi’kmaw partner in 2021 in a decision expected to have significant effect on the way judges consider Indigenous men who commit violent crimes against Indigenous women.




In

content:
C’est sur le territoire anishnabe de la communauté de Kitigan Zibi que l’expédition Mamu Nikantetau a débuté, cette année. Une traversée qui se veut une rencontre entre des participants de différentes nations et des allochtones.




Initiée par le Dr Stanley Vollant, l’expédition en est à sa 4e édition. Pour le Dr Vollant, « la réconciliation doit être plus qu’un simple mot ou un concept. » Mamu Nikantetau en innu veut dire « avançons ensemble ». Cette année, l’aventure s’est déroulée à pied mais surtout en rabaska pour un total de 350 kilomètres.




Un an avant l’expédition, Guylaine Gros-Louis s’entraînait déjà dans l’espoir de se joindre au groupe. Elle a appris la bonne nouvelle en juillet et s’est munie d’un entraîneur privé pour travailler le haut de son corps : « C’est la fierté de faire ce périple-là, c’est un dépassement de soi. »




« Si je peux être un exemple, une source de motivation pour d’autres personnes, pourquoi pas. »




Derrière sa participation se cache une quête d’équilibre des quatre sphères : « il y a des sphères qui sont plus fragilisées, puis c’est d’aller travailler là-dessus. »




Une marche symbolique a marqué le début de cette aventure de dix jours.




Dr Vollant : « une 2e journée plus chargée avec une traversée de la rivière des Outaouais, appelée la kichi sibi et occupée par les communautés anishnabee depuis des millénaires. »

title: Mi’kmaw lawyer says Ottawa is stalling on ending second-generation cut-off
content:
Nine months after the Senate voted unanimously to end the second-generation cut-off, the federal government must now decide what to do with Bill S-2.

The government bill was introduced in the Senate, where senators added an amendment the government wasn’t expecting and doesn’t want.

The amendment would force Ottawa to scrap the second-generation cut-off and replace it with a one-parent rule.

Pam Palmater, Mi’kmaw lawyer and chair in Indigenous governance at Toronto Metropolitan University, has testified on a number of occasions at federal committees on the issue.

“Every single First Nation person is affected by Bill C-31 and the second-generation cut-off,” Palmater told APTN News.

Bill C-31, passed in 1985, split people registered under the Indian Act into two legal classes.

A person under section 6(1) of the law can pass status to a child no matter who the other parent is. But a person under section 6(2) — “one parent” status — can pass it on only if the other parent is also registered as “status” under the Indian Act.

After two generations of parenting with someone who is not registered, the third generation is out. That is the second-generation cut-off.
